text: Our brains are not the wisest part of us.
plain: Your gut often knows before your head can explain it.

text: There is no more thriftless proceeding than to try and mend the measured pace of Time. Be careful, then, not to become its debtor.
plain: Rushing what needs time costs you more later than waiting would.

text: The most terrible misfortunes are also the most improbable and remote--the least likely to occur.
plain: The disasters you dread most are the ones least likely to happen.

text: What people commonly call Fate is, as a general rule, nothing but their own stupid and foolish conduct.
plain: Most of what people blame on fate is their own bad choices.

text: The most finished man of the world would be one who was never irresolute and never in a hurry.
plain: Be decisive, and never be rushed.

text: It is a cowardly soul that shrinks or grows faint and despondent as soon as the storm begins to gather, or even when the first cloud appears on the horizon.
plain: Do not fold at the first sign of trouble.

text: Our whole life itself--let alone its blessings--would not be worth such a cowardly trembling and shrinking of the heart.
plain: A life spent cringing is not worth having. Face it.

text: It should never be forgotten that misfortune, be it great or small, is the element in which we live.
plain: Trouble is the normal state of life, so stop being shocked by it.

text: Whatever fate befalls you, do not give way to great rejoicings or great lamentations; partly because all things are full of change, and your fortune may turn at any moment; partly because men are so apt to be deceived in their judgment as to what is good or bad for them.
plain: Do not get too high or too low. Things turn, and you cannot tell what is really good for you.

text: It is not ferocity but cunning that strikes fear into the heart and forebodes danger; so true it is that the human brain is a more terrible weapon than the lion's paw.
plain: The sharp mind is more dangerous than brute force.

text: I may be allowed to express the matter, briefly, thus: the world is glorious to look at, but dreadful in reality.
plain: Life looks beautiful from outside and is hard from inside.

text: In our early days we fancy that the leading events in our life, and the persons who are going to play an important part in it, will make their entrance to the sound of drums and trumpets; but when, in old age, we look back, we find that they all came in quite quietly, slipped in, as it were, by the side-door, almost unnoticed.
plain: The big turns in life arrive quietly. Notice them.

text: The wrong side is not so pretty as the right, but it is more instructive; it shows the way in which the threads have been worked together.
plain: The messy side of life teaches more than the pretty side.

text: It would be a great advantage to a young man if his early training could eradicate the idea that the world has a great deal to offer him.
plain: Expecting the world to hand you things sets you up for disappointment.

text: The chief result gained by experience of life is clearness of view.
plain: What experience really buys you is seeing things as they are.

text: To see how short life is, a man must have grown old, that is to say, he must have lived long.
plain: You only feel how short life is once a lot of it is gone, so act now.

text: We cram the years so full of projects that if we were to try and carry them all out, death would come prematurely though we reached the age of Methuselah.
plain: You plan more than a lifetime can hold. Pick what matters.

text: Sometimes we credit ourselves with a longing to be in some distant spot, whereas, in truth, we are only longing to have the time back again which we spent there--days when we were younger and fresher than we are now.
plain: You often miss a time, not a place.

text: The cheerfulness and vivacity of youth are partly due to the fact that, when we are ascending the hill of life, death is not visible: it lies down at the bottom of the other side.
plain: Youth feels free because death is out of sight. It is still there.

text: As long as we are young, people may tell us what they please! we look upon life as endless and use our time recklessly; but the older we become, the more we practice economy.
plain: Treat your time like it is limited now, not later.

text: If the chief feature of the earlier half of life is a never-satisfied longing after happiness, the later half is characterized by the dread of misfortune.
plain: First you chase happiness, then you just try to avoid pain.

text: Towards the close of life, much the same thing happens as at the end of a bal masqué--the masks are taken off. Then you can see who the people really are, with whom you have come into contact in your passage through the world.
plain: Time reveals who people really are.

text: The progress of life shows a man the stuff of which he is made.
plain: Years of living show you what you are made of.

text: Every generation, no matter how paltry its character, thinks itself much wiser than the one immediately preceding it, let alone those that are more remote.
plain: Every era thinks it knows better than the last. Stay humble.

text: To be poor when one is old, is a great misfortune.
plain: Build your money now so your later years are not a struggle.

text: Death is the great reservoir of Life. Everything comes from Orcus; everything that is alive now was once there. Could we but understand the great trick by which that is done, all would be clear!
plain: Life comes out of death and goes back to it. It is one cycle.

text: While the young man fancies that there is a vast amount of good things in the world, if he could only come at them, the old man is steeped in the truth of the Preacher's words, that all things are vanity--knowing that, however gilded the shell, the nut is hollow.
plain: What you chase looks better from far away than it is.

text: Each separate misfortune, as it comes, seems, no doubt, to be something exceptional; but misfortune in general is the rule.
location: On the Sufferings of the World
plain: Your bad luck feels special but it is normal for everyone.

text: No little part of the torment of existence lies in this, that Time is continually pressing upon us, never letting us take breath, but always coming after us, like a taskmaster with a whip.
location: On the Sufferings of the World
plain: Time never stops chasing you. That pressure is part of life.

text: A ship without ballast is unstable and will not go straight.
location: On the Sufferings of the World
plain: Some weight and difficulty keeps you steady.

text: It is a blessing that we do not know what is really going to happen.
location: On the Sufferings of the World
plain: Not knowing the future is a mercy. Keep going.

text: Life is a task to be done. It is a fine thing to say defunctus est; it means that the man has done his task.
location: On the Sufferings of the World
plain: Life is work, and the best thing to say at the end is that you finished it.

text: Of a truth, need and boredom are the two poles of human life.
location: On the Sufferings of the World
plain: You are either struggling for something or bored. Both are normal.

text: We are like lambs in a field, disporting themselves under the eye of the butcher, who chooses out first one and then another for his prey.
location: On the Sufferings of the World
plain: Good days hide how fragile things are. Do not get comfortable.

text: Pardon's the word to all! Whatever folly men commit, be their shortcomings or their vices what they may, let us exercise forbearance; remembering that when these faults appear in others, it is our follies and vices that we behold.
location: On the Sufferings of the World
plain: Go easy on people. Their faults are yours too.

text: If he has a soul above the common, or if he is a man of genius, he will occasionally feel like some noble prisoner of state, condemned to work in the galleys with common criminals; and he will follow his example and try to isolate himself.
location: On the Sufferings of the World
plain: If you are above the crowd you will feel out of place and want to be alone.

text: A man finds himself, to his great astonishment, suddenly existing, after thousands and thousands of years of non-existence: he lives for a little while; and then, again, comes an equally long period when he must exist no more.
plain: You get a short window between two long absences. Use it.

text: Of every event in our life we can say only for one moment that it is; for ever after, that it was. Every evening we are poorer by a day.
plain: Each day you spend is gone for good.

text: Unrest is the mark of existence.
plain: Restlessness is just what being alive is.

text: We are like a man running downhill, who cannot keep on his legs unless he runs on, and will inevitably fall if he stops; or, again, like a pole balanced on the tip of one's finger; or like a planet, which would fall into its sun the moment it ceased to hurry forward on its way.
plain: You stay up by moving. Stopping is how you fall.

text: In the first place, a man never is happy, but spends his whole life in striving after something which he thinks will make him so; he seldom attains his goal, and when he does, it is only to be disappointed; he is mostly shipwrecked in the end, and comes into harbor with masts and rigging gone.
plain: You chase a goal for happiness, reach it, and feel let down.

text: The scenes of our life are like pictures done in rough mosaic. Looked at close, they produce no effect. There is nothing beautiful to be found in them, unless you stand some distance off.
plain: Your life only looks good from a distance. Up close it is rough.

text: We look upon the present as something to be put up with while it lasts, and serving only as the way towards our goal.
plain: You treat today as a waiting room, and it is the actual life.

text: Of how many a man may it not be said that hope made a fool of him until he danced into the arms of death!
plain: Do not spend your whole life waiting on something that never comes.

text: Every satisfaction he attains lays the seeds of some new desire, so that there is no end to the wishes of each individual will.
plain: Getting what you want just makes you want more.

text: The first task is to win something; the second, to banish the feeling that it has been won; otherwise it is a burden.
plain: First you have to earn it, then you have to keep from going numb.

text: Human life must be some kind of mistake.
plain: Sometimes existence itself looks like a mistake.

text: It is only in the microscope that our life looks so big. It is an indivisible point, drawn out and magnified by the powerful lenses of Time and Space.
plain: Zoom out and your problems shrink to nothing.

text: Reason deserves to be called a prophet; for in showing us the consequence and effect of our actions in the present, does it not tell us what the future will be?
plain: Think through what your action leads to before you do it.

text: Hatred comes from the heart; contempt from the head; and neither feeling is quite within our control.
plain: You cannot simply decide to stop feeling hatred or contempt.

text: Contempt is not incompatible with indulgent and kindly treatment, and for the sake of one's own peace and safety, this should not be omitted; it will prevent irritation; and there is no one who cannot do harm if he is roused to it.
plain: You can look down on someone and still be polite. It keeps you safe.

text: Hypochondria shows itself in a perpetual hunting after things that vex and annoy, and then brooding over them.
plain: Stop hunting for things to be upset about and then chewing on them.

text: Any incident, however trivial, that rouses disagreeable emotion, leaves an after-effect in our mind, which for the time it lasts, prevents our taking a clear objective view of the things about us, and tinges all our thoughts: just as a small object held close to the eye limits and distorts our field of vision.
plain: One small annoyance can warp how you see everything. Step back.

text: What makes people hard-hearted is this, that each man has, or fancies he has, as much as he can bear in his own troubles.
plain: People are cold because they are carrying their own weight.

text: In my head there is a permanent opposition-party; and whenever I take any step or come to any decision--though I may have given the matter mature consideration--it afterwards attacks what I have done, without, however, being each time necessarily in the right.
plain: That voice second-guessing every choice is not always right.

text: In giving way to emotion of this violent kind, the greatest genius puts himself on a level with the commonest son of earth.
plain: Lose your temper and you are no better than anyone else.

text: Every man takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world.
plain: People think what they can see is all there is.

text: There is no doubt that many a man owes his good fortune in life solely to the circumstance that he has a pleasant way of smiling, and so wins the heart in his favor.
plain: A good smile gets people further than they deserve.

text: A doctor can cure everyone but himself; if he falls ill, he sends for a colleague.
plain: You are blind about your own case. Ask a friend.

text: In all that we do, we wish, more or less, to come to the end; we are impatient to finish and glad to be done. But the last scene of all, the general end, is something that, as a rule, we wish as far off as may be.
plain: We rush through everything except the one thing that ends it all.

text: Every parting gives a foretaste of death; every coming together again a foretaste of the resurrection.
plain: Saying goodbye feels like a small death, and reunion feels like coming back to life.

text: With people of only moderate ability, modesty is mere honesty; but with those who possess great talent, it is hypocrisy.
plain: If you are genuinely good, do not pretend you are not.

text: The scenes and events of long ago, and the persons who took part in them, wear a charming aspect to the eye of memory, which sees only the outlines and takes no note of disagreeable details. The present enjoys no such advantage, and so it always seems defective.
plain: The past looks better than it was, so today always loses the comparison.

text: It is a curious fact that in bad days we can very vividly recall the good time that is now no more; but that in good days, we have only a very cold and imperfect memory of the bad.
plain: On bad days you remember the good times. On good days you forget how bad it was.

text: Men need some kind of external activity, because they are inactive within.
plain: People who keep busy all the time are often avoiding their own head.
